analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell owners and independent shops the parts, software, and manuals needed to repair their own machines.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2022 with two Democratic sponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern tractors and combines are computers on wheels. When one breaks, the manufacturer controls the diagnostic software, repair parts, and security locks, so farmers often must wait for an authorized dealer instead of fixing the machine themselves or hiring a local independent shop. This bill would have required the manufacturers to sell those items on the same terms they offer their own dealers, let owners bypass digital locks to make repairs, and put a manufacturer's copyrights or patents into the public domain if it cut off supply. The Federal Trade Commission would have enforced it. The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease electronics-enabled equipment, and the independent repair shops that serve them. They would gain access on equal terms to the manuals, diagnostic software, parts, and tools that manufacturers currently reserve for their dealer networks, cutting repair costs and downtime during planting and harvest windows.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must offer any owner or independent repair provider the documentation, parts, software, and tools needed to diagnose, maintain, or repair electronics-enabled farm equipment, on terms at least as favorable as those given to their own authorized dealers.
Repair documentation must be provided at no charge, and software repair tools must be provided at no charge without requiring authorization or internet access to use.
Owners may bypass copyright protection locks when the purpose is diagnosing, maintaining, repairing, or upgrading their farm equipment, and may share or traffic in tools built for that purpose.

If a manufacturer stops supplying a required item to authorized repair providers, any copyright or patent it holds on that item goes into the public domain, and replacement parts must be installable without damaging the machine.
The Federal Trade Commission enforces the requirements, treating violations as unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of electronics-enabled farm equipment, such as tractor and combine makers, would lose revenue and control from their exclusive grip on parts, diagnostic software, and dealer service. Their authorized dealers would face new competition from independent shops and owner repairs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers

drawbacks.text: The bill limits the carve-out for safety and emissions: it does not allow permanently deactivating safety notification systems, changing settings to bring equipment out of compliance with safety or emissions laws, or evading emissions or copyright law, and manufacturers argue that access to security-lock tools invites tampering with exactly those systems.

The bill explicitly does not require manufacturers to divulge trade secrets beyond what is needed to supply repair materials on fair and reasonable terms, but manufacturers contend that releasing diagnostic software and repair data exposes proprietary designs; the bill answers this by requiring only fair-and-reasonable access rather than disclosure.

Enforcement depends entirely on FTC rulemaking and case-by-case action, and 'fair and reasonable terms' would be defined by regulation, so the practical protections depend on how the rules are written and enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers, the benefits are large and direct: a stuck combine during harvest can cost thousands of dollars a day in lost time, and the bill directly attacks the wait-for-the-dealer problem. The main costs fall on manufacturers' repair and parts margins, not on ordinary buyers in any obvious way, and the bill itself builds in guardrails for safety, emissions, and trade secrets. The honest weakness is enforcement: with no private right of action and everything hinging on FTC rules, the guarantee is only as strong as the regulator. The bill was also narrow, covering only agricultural equipment rather than all consumer products.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on February 1, 2022, joined by Sen. Ben Ray Luján as cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The bill received no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks are better off: they keep exclusive control of repair parts, diagnostic software, and security locks, and the service revenue that comes with it, while farmers still must go through authorized dealers for many repairs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 1, 2022 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers
against.role: Equipment makers with exclusive control of parts, software, and dealer repair networks
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair mandates for agricultural equipment, arguing that opening diagnostic software and security locks risks tampering, emissions violations, and exposure of proprietary technology.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded. The only recorded support was from two Democratic senators (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without any recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Farm equipment manufacturers (tractors, combines, and other electronics-enabled machinery)
industries.note: These manufacturers currently control diagnostic software, repair parts, security locks, and authorized dealer networks, which lets them charge for and channel nearly all repair work. The bill would have forced them to sell the same materials to owners and independent shops on dealer-level terms, ending that exclusive control.

Dealers would lose their near-exclusive service business to owner repairs and independent shops, though the bill explicitly does not require them to share their own materials — only the manufacturers.
The bill would have given independent shops the same access to parts, documentation, and software tools as manufacturer-authorized dealers, expanding their business.
